# Guess the Number with Duke

Duke, the Java mascot, is thinking of a whole number from 1 to 10. You get five
guesses. Guess right and Duke jumps for joy.

Built from [BRD.md](BRD.md), [java-prompt.txt](java-prompt.txt), and
[demo-prompt-common.md](demo-prompt-common.md), which are the copies of the
requirements and the generation prompt this project was built against.

## Running it

Every command here runs from this directory, not from the repository root. The
root holds one directory per demo and no POM of its own, so Maven has nothing to
build there.

```bash
cd java-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1
mvn package
java -jar target/java-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1.jar
```

Then open <http://localhost:8080/>.

The port comes from the first argument, then the `PORT` variable, then 8080:

```bash
java -jar target/java-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1.jar 9000
PORT=9000 java -jar target/java-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1.jar
```

Skip the packaging step during development:

```bash
mvn compile exec:java
```

## Running the tests

```bash
cd java-demo-claude-code-opus-5-1
mvn test
```

The suite checks the rules directly and then plays whole games over real HTTP
against a server on an ephemeral port. `GameApiEndToEndTest` and
`FrontEndEndToEndTest` play against a known secret so the win and lose paths are
deterministic; `RandomGameEndToEndTest` plays 25 real games by halving the range
from the high and low feedback, which only ever wins if that feedback is right.

## Requirements

Java 25 and Maven. There are no runtime dependencies: the server is the JDK's
own `com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer`, JSON is written by hand, and the front
end is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. JUnit is the only dependency at all, and
it is test-scoped.

## How it fits together

The server owns the game. The browser never learns the secret number until the
game is over, the guess limit is enforced server-side, and even the wording the
player reads comes down with the state, so the front end only draws what it is
told.

| Class | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `App` | Resolves the port and starts the server. |
| `GameServer` | The running game: HTTP server, virtual-thread executor, idle-session sweep. |
| `GameRules` | The three fixed numbers: 1, 10, and five guesses. |
| `GameRoute` | The three addresses the game answers on, each with its one method. |
| `GameState` | An immutable game at one moment, plus every transition. |
| `GuessingGame` | One player's game. Parses guesses and swaps state atomically. |
| `GameMessages` | The player-facing wording for a state. |
| `GameSessions` | One game per session cookie, swept once a player goes quiet. |
| `SessionCookie` | Mints and reads the cookie that identifies a browser. |
| `GameApiHandler` | The JSON API. |
| `StaticAssetHandler` | Serves the front end out of the jar. |
| `GameStateJson` / `JsonWriter` | Render state as JSON without a JSON library. |
| `SecretNumberPicker` | Draws the secret. Injected so tests can fix it. |

Each request is handled on a virtual thread, and a game's state lives in a
single `AtomicReference`, so two requests on one session can never interleave
into a half-applied guess. The server listens on the loopback address only, and
games whose players have been quiet for thirty minutes are swept; the number of
tracked games is capped so cookie-less requests cannot grow the map without
limit.

### API

| Request | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/game` | The current game, starting one if this browser has none. |
| `POST /api/game/new` | A fresh game. The page calls this on load, so a reload starts over. |
| `POST /api/game/guess` | The game after the guess. The body is the raw guess as plain text. |

Any other address answers 404 without claiming a session, and a known address
answers 405 with an `Allow` header when the method is wrong.

Every one of them answers with the whole state:

```json
{
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "feedback": "TOO_LOW",
  "message": "3 is too low. Try higher. 4 guesses left.",
  "guessesMade": 1,
  "guessesRemaining": 4,
  "guessLimit": 5,
  "lowestNumber": 1,
  "highestNumber": 10,
  "lastGuess": 3,
  "secretNumber": null
}
```

`status` is `ACTIVE`, `WON`, or `LOST`. `feedback` is `NONE`, `REJECTED`,
`TOO_HIGH`, `TOO_LOW`, or `CORRECT`; `REJECTED` means the submission was not a
whole number in range, so it did not count against the limit. `secretNumber`
stays `null` until the game is over.

### Front end

`index.html`, `styles.css`, and `app.js` live in `src/main/resources/web` and
are served from the classpath. Guesses can be entered and submitted with the
keyboard alone, the form is deliberately `novalidate` so the server's friendly
wording does the talking instead of a browser tooltip, and the result message is
a live region so screen readers announce it. Every text and control color clears
the 4.5:1 contrast benchmark in both the light and dark palettes.

Responses can arrive out of order, so each request takes a ticket and only the
newest one is allowed to draw. Without that, a slow guess could land after a
restart and put the finished game back on screen.

Duke is shown with the official artwork from the
[OpenJDK Duke project](https://github.com/openjdk/duke): `Thinking` while he is
thinking of the number, `Wave` when he celebrates. The only change to the
artwork is a cropped `viewBox`, so he scales without the original page margins.
The win animation is three CSS hops with a tilt over 1.5 seconds, ending back in
the resting pose; it runs once, never blocks the New game button, and is turned
off under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
